headline: Canada cannabis sales hit C$493.5M; Brazil passes 1.1M patients
dek: Statistics Canada data out 20 November show sales up 4.1% on the year, while a Kaya Mind report puts Brazil's 2026 medical market at R$1.14 billion.
key_points: Canadian licensed cannabis stores sold about C$493.5 million in September 2026, up 4.1% from a year earlier and down 5.2% from August's record C$520.4 million.
Sales for January to September reached about C$4.42 billion, roughly C$235 million more than the same period of 2025.
Brazil has 1.11 million medical cannabis patients, up 27% in a year, and a market worth R$1.14 billion in 2026, according to research firm Kaya Mind.
In Brazil, patient numbers are growing faster than revenue because prices are falling: a pharmacy bottle of oil averages R$650, down from R$735 in 2024.
body: Two sets of numbers released this week show two national cannabis markets at very different stages. Canada, eight years into legal adult-use sales, is growing in single digits. Brazil, which has only medical access and a patchwork of ways to get it, is adding patients at 27% a year.

Statistics Canada published September retail figures on Friday 20 November. Brazilian research firm Kaya Mind released the fifth edition of its Medical Cannabis Yearbook on 18 November. Both were reported by The Marijuana Herald.
## Canada: September down from a record, up on the year

Licensed cannabis retailers across Canada sold about C$493.5 million in September, according to Statistics Canada's Monthly Retail Trade Survey. That is about 4.1% more than the C$474 million recorded in September 2025, a gain of nearly C$20 million.
It is also about 5.2% less than August, when stores posted a record C$520.4 million. September ended a run of four straight months above C$500 million that began in May.

For the first nine months of 2026, sales came to roughly C$4.42 billion, against about C$4.19 billion in the same months of 2025. The Marijuana Herald rounds the gain to 6%. On the rounded figures it reports, an increase of about C$235 million works out to about 5.6%.
## Can Canada reach C$6 billion this year?

The Herald says the country is on pace to approach C$6 billion in 2026. Our arithmetic says approach is the right word. Nine months at C$4.42 billion is an average of about C$491 million a month. To finish the year at C$6 billion, stores would need about C$1.58 billion in the last three months, or roughly C$527 million a month. That is more than the best month on record.
If the final quarter instead matches the nine-month average, the year would end near C$5.9 billion. Either way it would be a record year, the Herald notes.

For licensed producers, the message is steady, modest growth at home. That fits what companies have been reporting. As we reported on 20 November, Decibel's third-quarter revenue rose 7% while its international sales reached a record: for several Canadian producers, the faster growth is in exports, not in domestic stores.
## Brazil: 1.11 million patients

Brazil's numbers are of a different kind. Kaya Mind estimates that 1.11 million people are receiving cannabis-based treatment, up 27% from 2025 and up 158% from about 430,000 in 2023. It is the first time the estimate has passed one million.

The firm projects a market of R$1.14 billion in 2026, up 17% on last year, rising to R$1.29 billion in 2027 and R$1.45 billion in 2028. Dividing this year's market by the patient count gives roughly R$1,030 per patient per year. That is our calculation from the report's two headline figures and it is an average across very different channels.
## Three ways in

Brazilian patients reach cannabis medicines by three main routes, and the report sizes each. Individual imports authorised by the health regulator Anvisa are the largest, serving about 457,000 patients, or 41%. Pharmacies and drugstores serve about 406,000, or 37%. Patient associations serve about 248,000, or 22%. More than 10,000 patients also hold court authorisation to grow their own.

Import authorisations are still climbing. Kaya Mind projects about 262,000 by the end of 2026, up 35% from the record 194,691 issued in 2025. Anvisa had issued 160,905 by the end of August. On those figures the pace would have to rise from about 20,100 a month in the first eight months to about 25,300 a month in the last four to meet the projection.

Telemedicine is doing much of the work. Among patients who import, 58% consult remotely with a doctor in another state. Since 2019, patients in 5,076 municipalities, about 91% of Brazil's cities, have used the import system.
> Brazil's patient count rose 27% and its market 17%. The gap between the two numbers is falling prices.
## Prices are falling

Revenue is growing more slowly than patient numbers because treatment is getting cheaper. The average pharmacy price of a bottle of cannabis oil fell from R$735 in 2024 to R$650 in 2026, a drop of about 12%. Association products average R$352 a bottle and individually imported products R$556.

Measured by cannabinoid content, the order changes. Imports are cheapest at R$0.26 per milligram, against R$0.35 through pharmacies and associations. For companies selling into Brazilian pharmacies, that is the competitive benchmark: the imported product is cheaper per dose even though the pharmacy bottle costs more.
## Associations, cultivation and public money

The report counts 401 active patient associations. A survey of 42 of them found at least 35 hectares under cultivation, 30% more than in 2025. In January, Anvisa approved rules allowing licensed domestic cultivation for pharmaceutical and scientific purposes and set a framework for associations, The Marijuana Herald notes. Domestic growing at scale would put further pressure on prices and on imports.

Government is also a buyer. Since 2015, federal, state and municipal governments have together spent about R$832.8 million supplying cannabis-based treatments, with state governments accounting for 91% of that.
## How to read the two together

Canada's figures are official retail sales collected by the national statistics agency. Brazil's are estimates and projections from a private research firm, built from regulator data, surveys and its own modelling. They are not directly comparable, and we have not converted currencies.

What they show side by side is where growth is. A mature adult-use market is adding about 6% a year. A medical-only market with imports, pharmacies and associations is adding patients at more than four times that rate, with prices falling as it grows. For exporters of finished medical products, Brazil's import channel, 457,000 patients and rising, is the number to note.
## What to watch

Statistics Canada's October figures should arrive in about a month, and the December figure, due early in 2027, will settle whether 2026 reaches C$6 billion. In Brazil, watch Anvisa's year-end count of import authorisations against Kaya Mind's 262,000 projection, and the first licences under the January cultivation rules.
